heading.en: What does the electricity bill count?

hook.en: Your electricity bill counts units. One unit is one kilowatt-hour: a 1000 W heater running for one hour.
hook.kn: ನಿಮ್ಮ ವಿದ್ಯುತ್ ಬಿಲ್ 'ಯೂನಿಟ್'ಗಳನ್ನು ಎಣಿಸುತ್ತದೆ. ಒಂದು ಯೂನಿಟ್ ಎಂದರೆ ಒಂದು ಕಿಲೋವ್ಯಾಟ್-ಗಂಟೆ: 1000 W ಹೀಟರ್ ಒಂದು ಗಂಟೆ ಉರಿದರೆ ಬಳಸುವ ಶಕ್ತಿ.

objectives.en: Explain why power is transmitted at high voltage.

narration.en: Your electricity bill counts units. One unit is one kilowatt-hour: a 1000 W heater running for one hour.
narration.kn: ನಿಮ್ಮ ವಿದ್ಯುತ್ ಬಿಲ್ 'ಯೂನಿಟ್'ಗಳನ್ನು ಎಣಿಸುತ್ತದೆ. ಒಂದು ಯೂನಿಟ್ ಎಂದರೆ ಒಂದು ಕಿಲೋವ್ಯಾಟ್-ಗಂಟೆ: 1000 W ಹೀಟರ್ ಒಂದು ಗಂಟೆ ಉರಿದರೆ ಬಳಸುವ ಶಕ್ತಿ.

body.en: When charge Q moves through a potential difference V, energy QV is converted. The rate is the power: $P = VI$. For a resistor this becomes $P = I^2R = V^2/R$, and appears as heat (Joule heating). Energy = Pt; the commercial unit is 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.
body.kn: ವಿದ್ಯುತ್ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ P = VI = I²R = V²/R; ರೋಧಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಇದು ಉಷ್ಣವಾಗಿ ಕಾಣುತ್ತದೆ. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

narration.en: Electrical power is V times I. In a resistor it is also I squared R, or V squared by R, and appears as heat. One kilowatt hour is 3.6 million joules.
narration.kn: ವಿದ್ಯುತ್ ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯ P = VI = I²R = V²/R; ರೋಧಕದಲ್ಲಿ ಇದು ಉಷ್ಣವಾಗಿ ಕಾಣುತ್ತದೆ. 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

narration.en: A charge ΔQ falling through a potential difference V loses energy V ΔQ, so the power delivered is P = VI. Using V = IR, the same power is I²R or V²/R: this is the Joule heating in the resistor. Example: a 60 W, 220 V bulb has R = 220²/60, about 807 ohm, and draws about 0.27 ampere. A power line sends P at voltage V: the current is P/V, so the loss in the line is P²R_c/V². That is why power is carried at many kilovolts and stepped down near our homes.

say.en: A charge ΔQ falling through a potential difference V loses energy V ΔQ, so the power delivered is P = VI.
Using V = IR, the same power is I²R or V²/R: this is the Joule heating in the resistor.
Example: a 60 W, 220 V bulb has R = 220²/60, about 807 ohm, and draws about 0.27 ampere.
A power line sends P at voltage V: the current is P/V, so the loss in the line is P²R_c/V².
That is why power is carried at many kilovolts and stepped down near our homes.

body.en: To deliver power P at voltage V the line carries I = P/V. The loss in line resistance R_c is $I^2R_c = P^2R_c/V^2$. Raising V greatly cuts the loss, so power is transmitted at very high voltages and stepped down by transformers near homes.
body.kn: P ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯವನ್ನು V ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಕಳುಹಿಸಿದರೆ ತಂತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ನಷ್ಟ P²R_c/V². ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಪ್ರಸರಣ ಮಾಡಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

narration.en: Sending power P at voltage V needs current P by V, and the line loss is P squared R by V squared. So power is sent at very high voltage to keep losses small.
narration.kn: P ಸಾಮರ್ಥ್ಯವನ್ನು V ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಕಳುಹಿಸಿದರೆ ತಂತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ನಷ್ಟ P²R_c/V². ಆದ್ದರಿಂದ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್‌ನಲ್ಲಿ ಪ್ರಸರಣ ಮಾಡಲಾಗುತ್ತದೆ.

caption.en: A battery drives a current through a key, an ammeter, a bulb and a resistor in series, with a voltmeter across the resistor.

narration.en: Turn the circuit around. The ammeter gives I and the voltmeter gives V across the resistor, so the power used there is simply V times I.

caption.en: A power station sends P megawatt through lines of resistance R_c at voltage V kilovolt. Current I = P/V; loss = I²R_c.

tryThis.en: Send 1 MW at 11 kV through 10 Ω: about 8 % is lost.
Now raise V to 33 kV: the loss falls to one-ninth.
Try sending 1 MW at just 2 kV. Why is that impossible in practice?

narration.en: A power station sends P megawatt through lines of resistance R_c at voltage V kilovolt. Current I = P/V; loss = I²R_c. Send 1 MW at 11 kV through 10 Ω: about 8 % is lost. Now raise V to 33 kV: the loss falls to one-ninth. Try sending 1 MW at just 2 kV. Why is that impossible in practice?

problem.en: A 1000 W heater is designed for 220 V. Find the current it draws, its resistance, and the energy it uses in 2 hours.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. A 1000 W heater is designed for 220 V. Find the current it draws, its resistance, and the energy it uses in 2 hours.

problem.en: Bulbs rated 100 W and 60 W (both for 220 V) are joined in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?

steps.en: R = V²/P: R₁₀₀ = 484 Ω, R₆₀ ≈ 807 Ω.
In series the same current flows, so P = I²R is larger for the larger R.
The 60 W bulb dissipates more power.

narration.en: Let us solve this together. Bulbs rated 100 W and 60 W (both for 220 V) are joined in series across 220 V. Which glows brighter?

body.en: Bulbs in series: the one with the lower rated wattage (higher R) glows brighter. Bulbs in parallel: the one with the higher rated wattage glows brighter.

narration.en: Which bulb is brighter?. Bulbs in series: the one with the lower rated wattage (higher R) glows brighter. Bulbs in parallel: the one with the higher rated wattage glows brighter.

mnemonic.en: Series → smaller watts shine; Parallel → bigger watts shine

points.en: High-voltage transmission cuts I²R line loss.
points.kn: ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಪ್ರಸರಣ I²R ನಷ್ಟವನ್ನು ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ.

homework.en: A house uses four 60 W bulbs for 5 hours a day. Find the units used in 30 days.

narration.en: Recap. P = VI = I²R = V²/R. 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. For fixed R, P ∝ V². High-voltage transmission cuts I²R line loss.
narration.kn: ಪುನರಾವರ್ತನೆ. P = VI = I²R = V²/R. 1 kWh = 1 ಯೂನಿಟ್ = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. ಸ್ಥಿರ R ಗೆ P ∝ V². ಹೆಚ್ಚಿನ ವೋಲ್ಟೇಜ್ ಪ್ರಸರಣ I²R ನಷ್ಟವನ್ನು ಕಡಿಮೆ ಮಾಡುತ್ತದೆ.
